                                           Asymmetric product of left braces and simplicity;




arXiv:1705.08493v1 [math.QA] 23 May 2017
                                              new solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation
                                                 D. Bachiller           F. Cedó           E. Jespers           J. Okniński


                                                                                   Abstract
                                                     The problem of constructing all the non-degenerate involutive set-
                                                 theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation recently has been reduced
                                                 to the problem of describing all the left braces. In particular, the classifi-
                                                 cation of all finite left braces is fundamental in order to describe all finite
                                                 such solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. In this paper we continue
                                                 the study of finite simple left braces with the emphasis on the applica-
                                                 tion of the asymmetric product of left braces in order to construct new
                                                 classes of simple left braces. We do not only construct new classes but
                                                 also we interpret all previously known constructions as asymmetric prod-
                                                 ucts. Moreover, a construction is given of finite simple left braces with a
                                                 multiplicative group that is solvable of arbitrary derived length.

                                           2010 MSC: 16T25, 20E22, 20F16.
                                           Keywords: Yang-Baxter equation, set-theoretic solution, brace, simple brace,
                                           asymmetric product.


                                           1    Introduction
                                           Rump [23] introduced braces to study a class of solutions of the Yang-Baxter
                                           equation, an important equation in mathematical physics (see [27, 21]). Recall
                                           that a set-theoretic solution of the Yang-Baxter equation is a map r : X ×X −→
                                           X × X, such that X is a non-empty set and

                                                                           r12 r23 r12 = r23 r12 r23 ,

                                           where rij denotes the map X × X × X −→ X × X × X acting as r on the (i, j)
                                           components and as the identity on the remaining component. The solution r
                                           is involutive if r2 = idX 2 , and it is non-degenerate if r(x, y) = (fx (y), gy (x))
                                           and fx and gy are bijective maps from X to X , for all x, y ∈ X. A systematic
                                           study of non-degenerate, involutive set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter
                                           equation (solutions of the YBE for short) was initiated in [13] and [17]. Solutions
                                           of this type have received a lot of attention in recent years (see for example
                                           [4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 18, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]).
                                               Every solution (X, r) of the YBE has associated two important groups: its
                                           structure group G(X, r) defined by the presentation hx ∈ X | xy = fx (y)gy (x)i


                                                                                       1
(where r(x, y) = (fx (y), gy (x))), and its permutation group G(X, r) = hfx | x ∈
Xi, a subgroup of SymX . There exists a homomorphism φ : G(X, r) −→ G(X, r)
such that φ(x) = fx , for all x ∈ X. Etingof, Schedler and Soloviev proved in
[13] that if (X, r) is a finite solution of the YBE, then G(X, r) and G(X, r) are
solvable groups.
    Rump introduced braces to study this type of solutions [23], and noted that
for every solution (X, r) of the YBE, the groups G(X, r) and G(X, r) have a
natural structure of left braces such that φ : G(X, r) −→ G(X, r) becomes a
homomorphism of left braces. A left brace is a set B with two operations, +
and ·, such that (B, +) is an abelian group, (B, ·) is a group and
                            a · (b + c) + a = a · b + a · c,
for all a, b, c ∈ B.
    In [4] a method is given to construct explicitly, given a left brace B, all the
solutions (X, r) of the YBE such that G(X, r) ∼    = B as left braces. Therefore,
the problem of constructing all the finite solutions of the YBE is reduced to
describing all the finite left braces. In particular, as a consequence of [4, Theo-
rem 3.1], every finite left brace is isomorphic to the left brace G(X, r), for some
finite solution (X, r) of the YBE. Therefore the multiplicative group of every
finite left brace is solvable. The finite solvable groups isomorphic to the mul-
tiplicative group of a left brace are called IYB groups [12]. Not all the finite
solvable groups are IYB groups. In fact, there exist finite p-groups (p a prime)
that are not of this type (see [2]). On the other hand, there are some known
classes of finite solvable groups that are IYB groups, (see [7, 12]). It is an open
problem whether every finite nilpotent group of class three is an IYB group.
    Every left brace B has a left action λ : (B, ·) −→ Aut(B, +), defined by
λ(b) = λb and λb (a) = b · a − b, for all a, b ∈ B (see [11, Lemma 1]). It is
called the lambda map of the left brace B. Note that, via the lambda map, the
additive structure of B is determined by the multiplicative structure of B and
vice-versa. It is known and easy to check that, in every left brace B, 0 = 1, i.
e. the neutral elements of the groups (B, +) and (B, ·) coincide. A left ideal of
a left brace B is a subgroup I of (B, +) such that λb (a) ∈ I, for all b ∈ B and
all a ∈ I. Note that, in this case, for x, y ∈ I, we have that
                 y −1 = −λy−1 (y) ∈ I     and xy = λx (y) + x ∈ I,
thus I also is a subgroup of (B, ·). An ideal of a left brace B is a normal
subgroup N of (B, ·) such that λb (a) ∈ N , for all b ∈ B and all a ∈ N . Note
that that, in this case, if x, y ∈ N , then
                −y = λy (y −1 ) ∈ N     and x + y = xλx−1 (y) ∈ N,
thus N also is a subgroup of (B, +), and hence it is a left ideal of B. A non-zero
left brace B is simple if {0} and B are the only ideals of B. We say that a left
brace B is trivial if a + b = a · b, for all a, b ∈ B.
    In order to classify all finite left braces, it is natural to start with classifying
the finite simple left braces. To build a foundation of the theory of finite simple

                                           2
braces it is crucial to find various methods of constructions of such structures and
to understand their common features. In this paper, we continue a systematic
approach to this fundamental problem, initiated in [6]. It is known that every
simple left brace of prime power order pn is a trivial brace of cardinality p, [23,
Corollary on page 166]. Until recently, these were the only known examples of
finite simple left braces. The first finite nontrivial simple left braces have been
constructed in [3, Theorem 6.3 and Section 7]; the additive groups of which
are isomorphic to Z/(p1 ) × (Z/(p2 ))k(p1 −1)+1 , where p1 , p2 are primes such that
p2 | p1 − 1 and k is a positive integer. In [6], using the iterated matched
product construction, we built new families of finite simple left braces of order
pn1 1 · · · pns s , where {p1 , . . . , ps } is any finite set of primes of cardinality greater
that 1 and n1 , . . . , ns are positive integers depending on the different primes
p1 , . . . , ps . It is remarkable that the derived length of the multiplicative group
of all the previously known simple left braces is at most 3.
      There are some known restrictions on the possible cardinalities of finite sim-
ple left braces (see [24]), but it is not at all clear which cardinalities may occur.
      In the study of finite simple groups the classification of all minimal simple
groups obtained by Thompson was of great significance (see [19, page 444]).
Recall that a minimal simple group is a finite non-commutative simple group
all of whose proper subgroups are solvable. Thus it seems natural to ask for
the meaning of a minimal non-trivial finite simple left brace. This should be
a non-trivial finite simple left brace such that all the factors of the composi-
tion series of every proper subbrace are trivial. In Section 2, we introduce the
concept of solvable left brace in a similar way as it is done in group theory.
Using this concept, a minimal non-trivial finite simple left brace is a non-trivial
simple left brace all of whose proper subbraces are solvable. We expect that the
classification of such finite simple left braces will be important in the further
study of finite simple left braces.
      In Sections 3 and 4, we recall the two main tools of the approach presented
in this paper: the asymmetric product of left braces and the wreath product
of left braces, respectively. We also prove some technical results useful for the
construction of new simple left braces.
      In Section 5, using the asymmetric product, we construct new classes of
simple left braces. Furthermore, we construct first examples of finite simple left
braces with a multiplicative group that is solvable of arbitrary derived length.
This is accomplished via the asymmetric product of special left braces, con-
structed using the wreath product, and trivial braces.
      In Section 6, we interpret all previously known constructions of finite left
braces as asymmetric products.


2     Solvable braces
As motivated in the introduction, in this section we define solvable left braces,
a class of left braces including all the left nilpotent left braces and all the right
nilpotent left braces, introduced in [9]. These concepts have some similarity


                                              3
with the corresponding concepts in group theory.
     Let B be a left brace. Consider the operation ∗ of B defined by a ∗ b :=
a · b − a − b = (λa − id)(b), for all a, b ∈ B. Rump in [23] introduced two series
of subbraces of B. One consists of left ideals B n , defined inductively as follows:
B 1 = B and
                                   m
                                   X
         B n+1 = B ∗ B n = {             ai ∗ bi | ai ∈ B, bi ∈ B n , for every i},
                                   i=1

for all positive integers n. Another one consisting of ideals B (n) , defined as
follows. B (1) = B and
                                    m
                                    X
      B (n+1) = B (n) ∗ B = {             ai ∗ bi | ai ∈ B (n) , bi ∈ B, for every i},
                                    i=1

for all positive integers n. Note that B (2) = B 2 , but in general B (3) and B 3 are
different because ∗ is not associative in general.
    We say that a left brace B is left nilpotent if there exists a positive integer
n such that B n = 0. A left brace B is right nilpotent if there exists a positive
integer such that B (n) = 0.
Remark 2.1 Smoktunowicz in [25, Theorem 1] proved that a finite left brace
B is left nilpotent if and only if its multiplicative group (B, ·) is nilpotent. In
particular, every left brace of order a power of a prime is left nilpotent.
    On the other hand, a left brace B is right nilpotent if and only if the solution
of the YBE associated with B is a multipermutation solution (see [9, Proposi-
tion 6]). Recall, if B is a left brace, its associated solution of the YBE is (B, r),
where
                             r(a, b) = (λa (b), λλ−1
                                                   a (b)
                                                         (a)),
for all a, b ∈ B. In particular, every non-zero right nilpotent left brace B has
non-zero socle, that is Soc(B) = {a ∈ B | a · b = a + b for all b ∈ B} 6= {0}.
    In [1] it is proved that there exist two left braces B1 and B2 of order 8
such that Soc(Bi ) = {0}. Therefore B1 and B2 are left nilpotent but not right
nilpotent.
    Consider the trivial left braces K = Z/(2)×Z/(2) and Z/(3). Let α : Z/(3) −→
Aut(K, +) be the action defined by α(x) = αx and
                                                    x
                                                 0 1
                            αx (y, z) = (y, z)          ,
                                                 1 1
for all x ∈ Z/(3) and all y, z ∈ Z/(2). Then the semidirect product B3 =
K ⋊ Z/(3) is a left brace which is not left nilpotent. Now we have
      ((y1 , z1 ), x1 ) ∗ ((y2 , z2 ), x2 )
        = ((y1 , z1 ), x1 ) · ((y2 , z2 ), x2 ) − ((y1 , z1 ), x1 ) − ((y2 , z2 ), x2 )
        = ((y1 , z1 ) + αx1 (y2 , z2 ), x1 + x2 ) − ((y1 , z1 ), x1 ) − ((y2 , z2 ), x2 )
        = (αx1 (y2 , z2 ) − (y2 , z2 ), 0),

                                                4
                                                          (2)
for all yi , zi ∈ Z/(2) and all xi ∈ Z/(3). Hence B3 = K × {0} and, since
                                                                (3)
((y1 , z1 ), 0) ∗ ((y2 , z2 ), x2 ) = ((0, 0), 0), we get that B3 = {0}. Therefore B3 is
right nilpotent.

     Recall that a trivial brace is a left brace B such that any a, b ∈ B satisfy
a · b = a + b. We also say that B has trivial structure. Thus B is a trivial brace
if and only if B 2 = {0}.
     Let B be a left brace. It was proven in [23, page 161] that B 2 is always an
ideal of B. Observe that B/B 2 has trivial brace structure because a · b − a − b =
a ∗ b ∈ B 2 . Moreover, if I is an ideal of B, B/I has trivial structure if and only
if B 2 ⊆ I.
     In particular, note that [(B, ·), (B, ·)] ≤ B 2 because (B/B 2 , ·) is abelian.

Definition 2.2 A solvable brace is any left brace B which has a series 0 =
B0 ⊆ B1 ⊆ · · · ⊆ Bm = B such that Bi is an ideal of Bi+1 , and such that
Bi+1 /Bi is a trivial brace for any i ∈ {0, 1, . . . , m − 1}.

   Using the same arguments as in group theory, one can prove the following
results.
Proposition 2.3 (Second Isomorphism Theorem). Let B be a left brace, let H
be a sub-brace of B, and let N be an ideal of B. Then, HN is a sub-brace of
B. Moreover,
                            HN/N ∼ = H/(H ∩ N ).

Proposition 2.4 (a) Define d1 (B) = B 2 , and di+1 (B) = di (B)2 for every
   positive integer i. Then, B is a solvable brace if and only if dk (B) = 0 for
   some k.
(b) Let B be a left brace, and let I be an ideal of B. If I and B/I are solvable
    braces, then B is also solvable.
(c) Any sub-brace, and any quotient of a solvable brace is solvable.

    The third property means that there are neither simple sub-braces nor simple
quotients in a solvable brace, except for the trivial simple braces Z/(p), where
p is a prime.

Remark 2.5 Note that for every left brace B, dn (B) ⊆ B n+1 ∩ B (n+1) . Hence
every left nilpotent left brace is solvable, and every right nilpotent left brace is
solvable. We have seen in Remark 2.1 that there exists a finite left nilpotent left
brace B1 which is not right nilpotent, and there exists a finite right nilpotent
left brace B3 which is not left nilpotent. Hence the left brace B1 × B3 is neither
left nilpotent nor right nilpotent. But clearly B1 × B2 is solvable.

   On the other extreme end, one can introduce the following class of braces.

Definition 2.6 A left brace B is called perfect if it satisfies B 2 = B.


                                           5
   For instance, every non-trivial simple left brace is perfect. The following
example shows that the converse is not true. So, this class should play an
important role in the approach towards a description of all finite left simple
braces, and should deserve a further study.

Example 2.7 Take B to be the simple left brace of order 24 defined in [3]. Since
the multiplicative group of B is isomorphic to S4 , we can define a morphism
α : (B, ·) → Aut(Z/(3)), given by the sign morphism of S4 . Then, the semidirect
product of braces Z/(3) ⋊ B with respect to α, where Z/(3) is considered as a
trivial brace, is a perfect brace which is not simple.


3      Asymmetric product
In this section we recall a construction of left braces introduced by Catino, Co-
lazzo and Stefanelli [8], the asymmetric product of two left braces. Furthermore
we give a result that can be used to construct new simple left braces using
asymmetric products.
    Let S and T be two (additive) abelian groups. Recall that a (normalized)
symmetric 2-cocyle on T with values in S is a map b : T × T −→ S such that
  (i) b(0, 0) = 0;
 (ii) b(t1 , t2 ) = b(t2 , t1 );
(iii) b(t1 + t2 , t3 ) + b(t1 , t2 ) = b(t1 , t2 + t3 ) + b(t2 , t3 ), for all t1 , t2 , t3 ∈ T .
As a consequence, we get that b(t, 0) = b(0, t) = 0, for all t ∈ T .
Theorem 3.1 ([8, Theorem 3]). Let T and S be two left braces. Let b : T ×
T −→ S be a symmetric 2-cocycle on (T, +) with values in (S, +), and let
α : (S, ·) −→ Aut(T, +, ·) be a homomorphism of groups such that

             s · b(t2 , t3 ) + b(t1 · αs (t2 + t3 ), t1 ) = b(t1 · αs (t2 ), t1 · αs (t3 )) + s,    (1)

where αs = α(s), for all s ∈ S and t1 , t2 , t3 ∈ T . Then the addition and
multiplication over T × S given by

                    (t1 , s1 ) + (t2 , s2 ) = (t1 + t2 , s1 + s2 + b(t1 , t2 )),

                          (t1 , s1 ) · (t2 , s2 ) = (t1 · αs1 (t2 ), s1 · s2 ),
define a structure of left brace on T × S. We call this left brace the asymmetric
product of T by S (via b and α) and denote it by T ⋊◦ S.
    Note that the lambda map of T ⋊◦ S is defined by

            λ(t1 ,s1 ) (t2 , s2 ) =   (λt1 αs1 (t2 ), λs1 (s2 ) − b(λt1 αs1 (t2 ), t1 )) ,          (2)

and its socle is

    Soc(T ⋊◦ S) = {(t, s) | λs = idS , λt ◦ αs = idT , b(t, t′ ) = 0 for all t′ ∈ T }.

                                                   6
Moreover, the subset T × {0} is a normal subgroup of (T ⋊◦ S, ·), and {0} × S
is a left ideal of T ⋊◦ S.
    A particular case of this theorem is when we assume that b is a symmetric
bilinear form. In this case, conditions (i)-(iii) are automatic, and condition (1)
becomes
                      λs (b(t2 , t3 )) = b(λt1 αs (t2 ), λt1 αs (t3 )),
which is equivalent to the two conditions:

                         λs (b(t2 , t3 )) = b(αs (t2 ), αs (t3 )),               (3)
                              b(t2 , t3 ) = b(λt1 (t2 ), λt1 (t3 )),             (4)

for all s ∈ S and t1 , t2 , t3 ∈ T .
    To study simplicity of left braces we will often make use of the following
result without any further explicit reference.

Lemma 3.2 ([6, Lemma 2.5]). Let B be a left brace. Let I be an ideal of B.
Then
                          (λa − id)(b) ∈ I,
for all a ∈ I and all b ∈ B.

Theorem 3.3 Let S be a simple non-trivial left brace. Let T be a trivial brace
and let T ⋊◦ S be an asymmetric product of T by S via b : T × T −→ S and
                                                                             ′
α : (S, ·) −→ Aut(T, +). Suppose that for every t ∈ T \ {0}  P there exists t ∈ T
                ′
such that b(t, t ) 6= 0. Then T ⋊◦ S is simple if and only if s∈S Im(αs −id) = T .

Proof. Let I be a non-zero ideal of T ⋊◦ S. Let (t, s) ∈ I be a nonzero element.
Suppose that s = 0. Then t 6= 0. There exists t′ ∈ T such that b(t, t′ ) 6= 0, and
we have

                (λ(t,0) − id)(t′ , 0) = (t, 0)(t′ , 0) − (t, 0) − (t′ , 0)
                                      = (t + t′ , 0) − (t + t′ , b(t, t′ ))
                                       = (0, −b(t, t′ )) ∈ I.

Hence we may assume that s 6= 0. Since S is a simple non-trivial left brace,
Soc(S) = {0}. So there exists s′ ∈ S such that λs (s′ ) 6= s′ . Note that

              (λ(t,s) − id)(0, s′ )   = (t, s)(0, s′ ) − (t, s) − (0, s′ )
                                      = (t, ss′ ) − (t, s + s′ )
                                      = (0, λs (s′ ) − s′ ) ∈ I \ {(0, 0)}.

Since S is a simple left brace, we easily get that {(0, y) | y ∈ S} ⊆ I. Let x ∈ T
and y, z ∈ S. We have

   (λ(0,y) − id)(x, z)   = (0, y)(x, z) − (0, y) − (x, z)
                         = (αy (x), yz) − (x, y + z)

     Let T ′ = y∈S Im(αy − id). We have that T ′ × S ⊆ I. It is clear that
T ′ × S is a subgroup of the additive group of T ⋊◦ S. Let (x, y) ∈ T ⋊◦ S and
(x′ , y ′ ) ∈ T ′ × S. Note that
                 λ(x,y) (x′ , y ′ ) =    (x, y)(x′ , y ′ ) − (x, y)
                                    =    (x + αy (x′ ), yy ′ ) − (x, y)
                                     =   (αy (x′ ), yy ′ − y − b(x, αy (x′ )))
and αy ◦ (αz − id) = (αyzy−1 − id) ◦ αy . Therefore λ(x,y) (x′ , y ′ ) ∈ T ′ × S.
Furthermore
     (x, y)(x′ , y ′ )(x, y)−1   =   (x + αy (x′ ), yy ′ )(−α−1
                                                             y (x), y
                                                                      −1
                                                                         )
                                 =   (x + αy (x′ ) − αyy′ y−1 (x), yy ′ y −1 ) ∈ T ′ × S.
Hence T ′ × S is an ideal of T ⋊◦ S. Thus T ⋊◦ S is simple if and only if T ′ = T ,
and the result follows.



4     Wreath products of left braces
In this section we recall the definition of the wreath product of left braces (see
[11, Corollary 1]) and we study how to construct automorphisms of wreath
products of left braces. The aim is to build new classes of left braces via the
iterated wreath product construction.
    Let G1 and G2 be left braces. Recall that the wreath product G2 ≀ G1 of the
left braces G2 and G1 is a left brace which is the semidirect product of left braces
H2 ⋊G1 , where H2 = {f : G1 −→ G2 | |{g ∈ G1 | f (g) 6= 1}| < ∞} is a left brace
with the operations (f1 · f2 )(g) = f1 (g) · f2 (g) and (f1 + f2 )(g) = f1 (g) + f2 (g),
for all f1 , f2 ∈ H2 and g ∈ G1 , and the action of (G1 , ·) on H2 is given by the
homomorphism σ : (G1 , ·) −→ Aut(H2 , +, ·) defined by σ(g)(f )(x) = f (g −1 x),
for all g, x ∈ G1 and f ∈ H2 . We will denote σ(g)(f ) simply by g(f ).
    As in group theory (see [20, Hilfssatz I.15.7(b)]), one can extend every au-
tomorphism of the left brace G1 to an automorphism of G2 ≀ G1 in a natural
way.
Proposition 4.1 Let G1 and G2 be two left braces. Let α1 ∈ Aut(G1 , +, ·).
Let H2 = {f : G1 −→ G2 | |{g ∈ G1 | f (g) 6= 1}| < ∞}. Let α     b1 : H2 −→ H2 be
                   b1 (f )(g) = f (α1−1 (g)), for all f ∈ H2 and all g ∈ G1 . Then
the map defined by α
the map α2 : G2 ≀ G1 −→ G2 ≀ G1 defined by α2 (f, g) = (b    α1 (f ), α1 (g)), for all
f ∈ H2 and all g ∈ G1 , is an automorphism of left braces.
Proof. The proof is similar to the proof of [20, Hilfssatz I.15.7(b)] and we leave
it to the reader.

   In the situation described above, we say that α2 is the automorphism of G2 ≀
G1 induced by the automorphism α1 of G1 . Thus, given left braces G1 , G2 , . . . , Gn ,

                                               8

the left brace
                      Gn ≀ (Gn−1 ≀ · · · (G2 ≀ G1 ) · · · ),
where αi is the automorphism of Gi ≀ (Gi−1 ≀ · · · (G2 ≀ G1 ) · · · ) induced by the
automorphism αi−1 of Gi−1 ≀ (Gi−2 ≀ · · · (G2 ≀ G1 ) · · · ) (as in Proposition 4.1),
for all n ≥ i ≥ 2.

Lemma 4.3 Let G be a finite group and let K be a field of characteristic p.
Suppose that p is not a divisor of the order of G. Consider the semidirect
product K[G] ⋊ G with respect to the action of G on the additive group of K[G]
by left multiplication. Let D0 = G and, for m > 0, let Dm = [Dm−1 , Dm−1 ].
Let E0 = K[G] ⋊ G and, for m > 0, let Em = [Em−1 , Em−1 ]. Then

                         Em = ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm ,                             (5)

for all m > 0. (Here ω(K[G]) denotes the augmentation ideal of the group
algebra K[G].) In particular, the derived length of E0 is d + 1, where d is the
derived length of G.

Proof. We shall prove the result by induction on m. For m = 1, we have that

                ((1 − h)α, 1) = (α, h−1 )−1 (0, h)−1 (α, h−1 )(0, h),

for all h ∈ G and α ∈ K[G], and

                   (0, h−1 g −1 hg) = (0, h)−1 (0, g)−1 (0, h)(0, g).

                                           9
Hence
                               ω(K[G]) ⋊ D1 ⊆ E1 .
On the other hand

        (α, h)−1 (β, g)−1 (α, h)(β, g)
          = (−h−1 α, h−1 )(−g −1 β, g −1 )(α + hβ, hg)
          =    (−h−1 α − h−1 g −1 β, h−1 g −1 )(α + hβ, hg)
          =    (−h−1 α − h−1 g −1 β + h−1 g −1 (α + hβ), h−1 g −1 hg)
          =    ((h−1 g −1 − h−1 )α + (h−1 g −1 h − h−1 g −1 )β, h−1 g −1 hg),

for all α, β ∈ K[G] and all h, g ∈ G. Hence E1 ⊆ ω(K[G]) ⋊ D1 . Therefore
E1 = ω(K[G]) ⋊ D1 .
    Suppose that m > 1 and that (5) holds for m−1. Let α ∈ ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G].
We have
                ((1 − h)α, 1) = (α, h−1 )−1 (0, h)−1 (α, h−1 )(0, h),
for all h ∈ Dm−1 . Thus

        ω(K[Dm−1 ])ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] × {1}
           ⊆ [ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm−1 , ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm−1 ].

Since p is not a divisor of |G|, the group algebras K[Dj ] are semisimple by
Maschke’s Theorem, for all non-negative integers j. Hence

              ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[Dm−2 ] = ω(K[Dm−1 ])ω(K[Dm−2 ]),

and consequently

              ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[G] = ω(K[Dm−1 ])ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G],

if m > 1. Hence

        ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm
          ⊆    [ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm−1 , ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm−1 ]
          =    [Em−1 , Em−1 ] (by the induction hypothesis)
          =    Em .

Since

        (α, h)−1 (β, g)−1 (α, h)(β, g)
             = ((h−1 g −1 − h−1 )α + (h−1 g −1 h − h−1 g −1 )β, h−1 g −1 hg),

for all α, β ∈ ω(K[Dm−2 ])K[G] and all h, g ∈ Dm−1 , we also have that

                          Em ⊆ ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm ,

and therefore Em = ω(K[Dm−1 ])K[G] ⋊ Dm . Thus the result follows.



                                         10
5     New simple left braces
In [3], Bachiller gave the first examples of non-trivial finite simple left braces.
They are of order pn1 1 p2 for any pair of primes p1 , p2 such that p1 divides p2 − 1,
and n1 is a positive integer that depends on p2 . In [6], for every s > 1 and
every set {p1 , . . . , ps } of s distinct primes, the authors constructed examples of
finite simple left braces of order pn1 1 · · · pns s for some positive integers n1 , . . . , ns
depending on the pi ’s.
    In this section we generalize the construction of simple left braces of [3].
Moreover, using the iterated wreath product construction, we give examples of
finite simple left braces with multiplicative group of arbitrary derived length.
Note that the multiplicative groups of all the previously known finite simple left
braces [3, 6] have derived length at most 3.

5.1     Finite simple left braces with multiplicative group of
        arbitrary derived length
Let R be a ring. We will consider the trivial brace associated to R, which is
(R, +, +). Let G be a left brace. Note that the trivial left brace

                   H = {f : G −→ R | |{x ∈ G | f (x) 6= 0}| < ∞}

can be identified with the trivial left brace associated to the group ring R[G] by
                                        X
                                  f=        f (x)x,
                                           x∈G

for all f ∈ H. We know that the wreath product of left braces R ≀ G is the
semidirect product H ⋊ G with respect to the action defined by g(f )(x) =
f (g −1 x) for all x, g ∈ G and f ∈ H. Note that with the above identification
this action is
                         X                X             X
                 g(f ) =    f (g −1 x)x =   f (x)gx = g   f (x)x,
                          x∈G                 x∈G               x∈G

so it coincides with the left multiplication by g ∈ G in the group ring R[G].
Thus R ≀ G can be identified with the semidirect product R[G] ⋊ G with respect
to the action given by left multiplication.
     Let n be an integer greater than 1. Let p1 , . . . , pn be distinct prime numbers.
Consider the trivial braces associated to the fields Fpi of order pi , for i =
1, . . . , n. Sometimes we will need to use the ring product of Fpi . In order to
avoid confusion, we always denote this product by a dot.
     We shall define recursively two series of left braces Gj and Gj , for j =
1, . . . , n, in such a way that Gj is defined as a quotient of Gj , and that Gj+1
is defined as a wreath product. First of all, let G1 = G1 = Fp1 . By recurrence
we define the Gj ’s, for 2 ≤ j ≤ n, as Gj = Fpj ≀ Gj−1 . For this to make sense,
we must define next Gj as a quotient of Gj . Let Hj = {f : Gj−1 −→ Fpj } be


                                              11
the set of all the functions from Gj−1 to Fpj . Since Fpj is a trivial brace, so
is Hj (for the pointwise addition of functions). Let Ij = {f : Gj−1 −→ Fpj |
f is a constant map}. Clearly Ij is an ideal of Hj . By the definition of wreath
product, we know that Gj = Hj ⋊ Gj−1 . Let

                                Nj = {(f, 0) ∈ Gj | f ∈ Ij }.

Note that Nj is a central subgroup of the multiplicative group of the left brace
Gj . Indeed, for (f1 , 0) ∈ Nj and (f2 , g) ∈ Gj , we have

           (f2 , g)(f1 , 0) = (f2 + g(f1 ), g) = (f2 + f1 , g) = (f1 , 0)(f2 , g),

where the second equality holds because f1 is a constant map. Furthermore,
since

     λ(f1 ,0) (f2 , g) = (f1 , 0)(f2 , g) − (f1 , 0) = (f1 + f2 , g) − (f1 , 0) = (f2 , g),

we have that Nj ⊆ Soc(Gj ). Thus Nj is an ideal of the left brace Gj . We define
Gj = Gj /Nj . Let H j = Hj /Ij . It is clear that Gj = H j ⋊ Gj−1 . Hence

                    Gn = H n ⋊ (H n−1 ⋊ (· · · ⋊ (H 2 ⋊ Fp1 ) . . . )),

and, therefore, every element in Gn is of the form

                                   (hn , hn−1 , . . . , h2 , c),

where hj ∈ H j denotes the class of hj ∈ Hj modulo Ij , and c ∈ Fp1 .
  Note that |G1 | = |Fp1 | = p1 and, for 2 ≤ j ≤ n,
                                                             |G    |
                                       |Gj |   |Gj−1 |pj j−1
                             |Gj | =         =               .
                                       |Nj |        pj
                            m
Thus |Gj | = p1 pm         j
                 2 · · · pj , for some positive integers m2 , . . . , mj .
                   2




   Now we introduce some actions and some bilinear forms in order to apply the
asymmetric product construction to the braces Gj . Suppose that pj is a divisor
of pi − 1 for all 2 ≤ j ≤ n and all 1 ≤ i < j. The existence of such primes is
a consequence of Dirichlet’s Theorem on arithmetic progressions. Let A be the
trivial brace associated to the ring Fp2 × · · · × Fpn . Then a = (1, . . . , 1) is a
generator of the trivial brace A. Besides the brace structure, A is a ring, and
we will use this structure sometimes. Again we will denote this ring product as
a dot.
    Since pj is a divisor of p1 − 1, for all 2 ≤ j ≤ n, there exists γ ∈ (Fp1 )∗ of
order p2 · · · pn . Let α1 (ia) be the automorphism of the left brace Fp1 defined
by α1 (ia)(z) = γ i · z, for all z ∈ Fp1 , and i ∈ Z. Since the additive order
of a is p2 · · · pn , α1 (ia) is well-defined. By Proposition 4.1, α1 (ia) induces an
automorphism α2 (ia) of the left brace G2 . Recall that

                        α2 (ia)(h2 , c) = (b
                                           α1 (ia)(h2 ), α1 (ia)(c)),

and
                                   b1 (ia)(h2 )(d) = h2 (α1 (ia)−1 (d)).
                                   α

α′2 (a)i . Hence, the map α′2 : A −→ Aut(G2 , +, ·) is a morphism of groups. By

                                                                           

                     bj (f1 , f2 ) = εj (f1 ) · εj (f2 ) − εj (f1 • f2 ),

for all hj , h′ j ∈ H j , 2 ≤ j ≤ n, and all z1 , z1′ ∈ Fp1 . It is easy to see that b is
bilinear.
    In order to apply Theorem 3.1, we need to check that the bilinear form b
satisfies conditions (3) and (4). As a first step, we will check the analogous
property for bj .

Lemma 5.1 Let h1 , h2 ∈ Hj and g ∈ Gj−1 . Then

                           bj (h1 , h2 ) = bj (b
                                               αj−1 (a)(h1 ) , α

(recall that a = (1, . . . , 1) is a generator of the trivial brace A) and

                                     bj (h1 , h2 ) = bj (g(h1 ) , g(h2 )),

where g(h) : Gj−1 −→ Fpj is the map defined by (g(h))(g ′ ) = h(g −1 g ′ ), for all
g ′ ∈ Gj−1 and h ∈ Hj .

                                                          13
Proof. The right side of the first equality is by definition

          bj (b
              αj−1 (a)(h1 ), α

                                                 − εj (b
                                                       αj−1 (a)(h1 ) • α
                                                                       bj−1 (a)(h2 )).

The action of αbj−1 (a) over a map f is a permutation of its images. Thus εj (f ),
which is the sum of all the images of f , is invariant under this action. Therefore,

          bj (b
              αj−1 (a)(h1 ), α

   The proof of the second equality is analogous, because the action of g ∈ Gj−1
over a map is also a permutation of its images.

    From the previous lemma, we are going to deduce the desired result for b.

Lemma 5.2 Let g1 , g2 , x ∈ Gn . Then

                            b(g1 , g2 ) = b(α′n (a)(g1 ), α′n (a)(g2 )),

   Since A is a trivial brace, by Lemma 5.2 and Theorem 3.1, we can construct
the asymmetric product Gn ⋊◦ A (via b and α′n ).
   Recall from (2) that, for (g, c), (g ′ , c′ ) ∈ Gn ⋊◦ A,
                λ(g,c) (g ′ , c′ ) = (λg α′n (c)(g ′ ) , c′ − b(λg α′n (c)(g ′ ), g)) .

    Consider the semidirect product of left braces Fpj [Gj−1 ] ⋊ Gj−1 with respect
to the action of Gj−1 on the additive group of the group ring Fpj [Gj−1 ] (con-
sidered as a trivial brace) by left multiplication. As mentioned above, we may
identify Fpj ≀ Gj−1 with Fpj [Gj−1 ] ⋊ Gj−1 .

Theorem 5.3 The left brace Gn ⋊◦ A is simple and the derived length of its
multiplicative group is n + 1.
                                                                        P
Proof. In this proof we shall identify Hj with Fpj [Gj−1 ] (via f = g∈Gj−1 f (g)g,
                                                    P
for all f ∈ Hj ). Thus Hj = Fpj [Gj−1 ], Ij = { g∈Gj−1 zg | z ∈ Fpj }. As usual,
we denote by h the natural image of h ∈ Hj in H j = Hj /Ij .
    Note also that, for j = 2, . . . , n, Hj , H j and A are trivial braces. In order
to avoid confusion, we only use the sum operation for these trivial braces. We
will only use the multiplication of the trivial brace G1 for elements in the group
ring H2 . Thus the product in Hj will mean the product in the corresponding
group ring.
    We shall prove the simplicity of the left brace Gn ⋊◦ A by induction on n.
For n = 2, let I be a nonzero ideal of G2 ⋊◦ A. Let (h2 , z1 , c) ∈ I be a nonzero
element, where h2 ∈ H 2 , z1 ∈ G1 and c ∈ A . We consider three mutually
exclusive cases.
    Case 1. Suppose that h2 6= 0. Then p1 (h2 , z1 , c) = (p1 h2 , 0, c′ ) ∈ I, for some
 ′
c ∈ A and p1 h2 6= 0, because H 2 has order a power of p2 . Thus we may assume
that (h2 , 0, c) ∈ I and h2 6= 0. Since b′2 is non-degenerate, there exists h ∈ H 2
such that b′2 (h2 , h) 6= 0. Hence
         λ(h,0,0) (h2 , 0, c) − (h2 , 0, c) = (h2 , 0, c − b′2 (h2 , h)) − (h2 , 0, c)
                                                = (0, 0, −b′2 (h2 , h)) ∈ I.

                                                   15
Since A has order p2 and b′ (h2 , h) ∈ A \ {0}, we have that {0} × {0} × A ⊆ I.
In particular (0, 0, a) ∈ I, where a = 1 is the fixed generator of A. Thus

                    λ(0,0,a) (0, z, 0) − (0, z, 0) = (0, (γ − 1)z, 0) ∈ I,

for all z ∈ G1 . Since γ−1 is a nonzero element of Fp1 , we have {0}×G1 ×{0} ⊆ I.
Hence {0} × G1 × A ⊆ I. Now we have

            (λ(0,z,0) − id)(h, 0, 0) = ((z − 1)h, 0, −b′2((z − 1)h, h)) ∈ I,

for all h ∈ H 2 and z ∈ G1 . Hence
                               X

                                     z∈G1

for all h ∈ H2 . Therefore π2 (ω(Fp2 [G1 ])) × G1 × A ⊆ I, where π2 : H2 −→ H 2
is the natural map. Note that

                              I2 + ω(Fp2 [G1 ]) = Fp2 [G1 ] = H2 .

Therefore H 2 × G1 × A ⊆ I. This implies that G2 ⋊◦ A = I in this case.
   Case 2. Suppose that h2 = 0 and z1 6= 0. Now p2 (0, z1 , c) = (0, p2 z1 , 0) ∈ I
and p2 z1 6= 0 because G1 has order p1 . Now

for all h ∈ H 2 . In particular, for h = 1 in the group ring H2 , we have

    Case 3. Suppose that (h2 , z1 ) = 0 and c 6= 0. Then (0, 0, a) ∈ I and, as in

    Therefore for n = 2 the left brace G2 ⋊◦ A is simple.
    Suppose now that n > 2 and assume that the result holds for n − 1. Let

three mutually exclusive cases.
    Case i. Suppose that hn 6= 0. Then

         p1 · · · pn−1 (hn , . . . , h2 , z1 , c) = (p1 · · · pn−1 hn , 0, . . . , 0, 0, c′ ) ∈ I

In particular (0, . . . , 0, (0, . . . , 0, 1)) ∈ I. Thus

Therefore Gn ⋊◦ A = I in this case.
   Case ii. Suppose that hn = 0 and (hn−1 , . . . , h2 , z1 ) 6= 0. Since the subbrace

   Case iii. Suppose that (hn , . . . , h2 , z1 ) = 0 and c 6= 0. In this case

           (λ(0,...,0,c) − id)(0, . . . , 0, z, 0) = (0, . . . , 0, α1 (c)(z) − z, 0) ∈ I,

for all z ∈ Fp1 . Since α1 (c) 6= id, by Case ii, Gn ⋊◦ A = I, again as desired.
    Therefore Gn ⋊◦ A is simple.
    In the remainder of the proof we show that the derived length of the mul-
tiplicative group of the left brace Gn ⋊◦ A is n + 1. Recall that this group is
the semidirect product Gn ⋊ A (via the action α′n ) of the multiplicative groups
of the left braces Gn and A (recall that A is the trivial brace associated to the
ring Fp2 × · · · × Fpn , and therefore the multiplicative group of the trivial brace A
coincides with its additive group). First we shall prove by induction on n that

                                [Gn ⋊ A, Gn ⋊ A] = Gn × {0}.

Suppose that n = 1. Note that if z1 ∈ G1 , then

       [(1, a)−1 , (z1 , 0)−1 ] = (1, a)(z1 , 0)(1, a)−1 (z1 , 0)−1 = ((γ − 1) · z1 , 0).

Hence [G1 ⋊ A, G1 ⋊ A] = G1 × {0}. Suppose that n ≥ 2 and that

                      [Gn−1 ⋊ An−1 , Gn−1 ⋊ An−1 ] = Gn−1 × {0}.

Let gn−1 ∈ Gn−1 and hn ∈ H n . Since the left brace Hn is trivial, we will use
the additive notation on Hn . Then
                                                             −1
                       [(0, gn−1 , 0), (hn , 1, 0)] = ((1 − gn−1 )hn , 1, 0).


                                                      17
Thus
               πn (ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ])) × {1} × {0} ⊆ [Gn ⋊ A, Gn ⋊ A].
By (6), which is also true for n = 2, we obtain that

                       H n × {1} × {0} ⊆ [Gn ⋊ A, Gn ⋊ A].

Since
                   [Gn−1 ⋊ An−1 , Gn−1 ⋊ An−1 ] = Gn−1 × {0},
we get that
                      H n × Gn−1 × {0} ⊆ [Gn ⋊ A, Gn ⋊ A]
and thus
                           [Gn ⋊ A, Gn ⋊ A] = Gn × {0},
as claimed. Hence, it is enough to show that the derived length of the multi-
plicative group Gn is n. It is clear that the derived length of G2 is 2. Sup-
pose that n > 2 and that Gn−1 has derived length n − 1. Recall that Gn =
Fpn [Gn−1 ] ⋊ Gn−1 . Hence, by Lemma 4.3, the derived length of Gn is n. Note
that Nn = In × {1} is a central subgroup of Gn = Hn ⋊ Gn−1 , and by (6)

                         Gn = Nn (ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ]) ⋊ Gn−1 ).

Furthermore, it is easy to see that

                       Nn ∩ (ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ]) ⋊ Gn−1 ) = {1}.

Since
                      Gn = Gn /Nn ∼
                                  = ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ]) ⋊ Gn−1 ,
and

      [Gn , Gn ] = [ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ]) ⋊ Gn−1 , ω(Fpn [Gn−1 ]) ⋊ Gn−1 ] ∼
                                                                    = [Gn , Gn ],

the derived length of Gn also is n and the result follows.


5.2     A generalized construction of simple braces
In this subsection we present a broad class of simple left braces, extending the
construction of [3]. Let A = Z/(l1 ) × · · · × Z/(ls ) be a finite abelian group and
let p be a prime such that p | q − 1 for every prime divisor q of the order of A.
For every i = 1, . . . , s, let
  1. bi be a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form over (Z/(p))ni ,
  2. fi and ci be elements of order p and li respectively in the orthogonal group
     of bi ,
  3. γi ∈ Z/(li ) be an invertible element of order p.

                                          18
Assume that
  (i) fi ci = cγi i fi ,
  (ii) γi − 1 is invertible in Z/(li ).
Put n = n1 + · · · + ns . Let T = (Z/(p))n ⋊ A be the semidirect product of the
trivial braces (Z/(p))n and A via the action

                                           β : A −→ Aut((Z/(p))n )

defined by β(a1 ,...,as ) (u1 , . . . , us ) = (ca1 1 (u1 ), . . . , cas s (us )), where β(a1 , . . . , as ) =
β(a1 ,...,as ) , for all ai ∈ Z/(li ) and all ui ∈ (Z/(p))ni .

Lemma 5.4 The map α : (Z/(p), +) −→ Aut(T, +, ·) defined by

           αµ (u1 , . . . , us , a1 , . . . , as ) = (f1µ (u1 ), . . . , fsµ (us ), γ1µ a1 , . . . , γsµ as ),

where α(µ) = αµ , for all µ ∈ Z/(p), all ai ∈ Z/(li ) and all ui ∈ (Z/(p))ni , is a
homomorphism of groups.

Proof. It is clear that αµ ∈ Aut(T, +). Because fi ci = cγi i fi for all i = 1, . . . , s,
it is straightforward to verify that αµ also is a multiplicative group homomor-
phism, and thus a brace homomorphism. Hence, α is a homomorphism.

    Let b : T × T −→ Z/(p), defined by

for all ui ∈ (Z/(p))ni and all ai ∈ Z/(li ). Since each bi is a symmetric bilinear

    We shall see that α and b satisfy condition (1). In this case this is equivalent

                                     b(t2 , t3 ) = b(αµ (t2 ), αµ (t3 )),                                               (7)

of T by Z/(p) via b and α.

                                                                 20
Theorem 5.7 The left brace B = T ⋊◦ Z/(p) is simple if and only if Im(ci −

I ′ defined in the previous lemma. So let I be a nonzero ideal of B. Let

          p(u1 , . . . , us , a1 , . . . , as , µ) =         (pu1 , . . . , pus , pa1 , . . . , pas , µ′ )

for some µ′ ∈ Z/(p), and pai 6= 0 because the order of A is not a multiple of the

           p(0, . . . , 0, pa1 , . . . , pas , µ′ ) = (0, . . . , 0, p2 a1 , . . . , p2 as , 0) ∈ I,

and p2 ai 6= 0. Thus we may assume that (0, . . . , 0, a1 , . . . , as , 0) ∈ I and ai 6= 0.
Let vi ∈ (Z/(p))ni and for j 6= i, let vj = 0 ∈ (Z/(p))nj . Then

        (v1 , . . . , vs , 0, . . . , 0, 0)−1 (0, . . . , 0, a1 , . . . , as , 0)(v1 , . . . , vs , 0, . . . , 0, 0)
           =      (−v1 , . . . , −vs , 0, . . . , 0, 0)(ca1 1 (v1 ), . . . , cas s (vs ), a1 , . . . , as , 0)
           =      ((ca1 1 − id)(v1 ), . . . , (cas s − id)(vs ), a1 , . . . , as , 0) ∈ I.

Since ci has order li and ai 6= 0, there exists vi ∈ (Z/(p))ni such that (cai i −
id)(vi ) 6= 0. Now

        ((ca1 1 − id)(v1 ), . . . , (cas s − id)(vs ), a1 , . . . , as , 0) − (0, . . . , 0, a1 , . . . , as , 0)
                    = ((ca1 1 − id)(v1 ), . . . , (cas s − id)(vs ), 0, . . . , 0, 0) ∈ I.

Thus we may assume that (0, . . . , 0, ui , 0, . . . , 0, 0, . . . , 0, 0) ∈ I for some nonzero

such that bi (wi , ui ) 6= 0. We have that

                           (λ(0,...,0,ui ,0,...,0,0,...,0,0) − id)(0, . . . , 0, wi , 0, . . . , 0, 0, . . . , 0, 0)

   Case 2: suppose that aj = 0 for all j. Thus (u1 , . . . , us , 0, . . . , 0, µ) ∈ I is a

5.3       Concrete construction of simple left braces
In this section we give concrete realisations of simple braces as constructed in

Remark 5.8 In our approach we exploited the bilinear form with matrix B =
(bij ), where bii = 0 and bij = 1 for i 6= j. Every permutation matrix is in the
orthogonal group of this bilinear form. In the concrete constructions we show
how to construct an element f in the orthogonal group that has the desired
properties. However, one can give a general reason why such elements exist.
     Assume that q and p are prime numbers such that p | (q − 1). Let c ∈ Sn
be an element of the symmetric group Sn for some n. Assume that c has order
q. Assume also that γ ∈ Z∗q has order p. We claim that cγ = f cf −1 for a
permutation f ∈ Sn of order p.
     Notice that cγ also has order q (since p, q are relatively prime) and in fact
    γ
c, c are products of the same number of disjoint cycles of length q. It is then
enough to consider the case where c = (1, 2, . . . , q), a cycle of length q, and
n = q. In particular, there exists g ∈ Sq such that gcg −1 = cγ . By the
hypothesis, γ p = qr + 1 for some nonnegative integer r. Then
                                                           p
                                        g p cg −p = cγ = cqr+1 = c.

It is easy to see that the centralizer CSq (c) of c in the symmetric group Sq is
equal to the cyclic group hci. Therefore g p ∈ hci. In particular, g pq = 1. Since
p | (q − 1), it follows that q = pk + 1 for some k and then g q = g pk+1 ∈ gCSq (c).
Therefore, g q cg −q = gcg −1 = cγ .
    Notice that g q 6= 1, as otherwise cγ = c, a contradiction, because c has order
q and γ ∈ Z∗q has order p. Therefore, g q 6= 1 and then g q is a permutation of
order p. Hence, we may put f = g q .



                                                           24
6     Other simple left braces as asymmetric prod-
      uct of left braces
Our aim in this section is to show that all previously known nontrivial left simple
braces (see [6, Theorems 3.1 and 3.6]) can be interpreted as asymmetric products
of braces. This sheds a new light on these classes of examples and raises the
question of a further application of the asymmetric product construction in the
context of the challenging program of finding new (simple) left braces.
    Let H(pr , n, Q, f ) be the left brace described in [6, Theorem 3.1], where p is
a prime number, r, n are positive integers, Q is a quadratic form over (Z/(pr ))n
(considered as a free module over the ring Z/(pr )) and f is an element in the
                                      ′
orthogonal group of Q of order pr for some 0 ≤ r′ ≤ r.
    Recall that the additive group of H(pr , n, Q, f ) is the additive abelian group
(Z/(pr ))n+1 . The elements of (Z/(pr ))n+1 will be written in the form (~x, µ),
with ~x ∈ (Z/(pr ))n and µ ∈ Z/(pr ). The lambda map of H(pr , n, Q, f ) is defined
by

               λ(~x,µ) (~y , µ′ ) = (f q(~x,µ) (~y ), µ′ + b(~x, f q(~x,µ) (~y ))),    (9)

for (~x, µ), (~y , µ′ ) ∈ (Z/(pr ))n+1 , where q(~x, µ) = µ − Q(~x), and b is the bilinear
form b(~x, ~y ) = Q(~x + ~y) − Q(~x) − Q(~y ) associated to Q.
    Let T be the trivial brace (Z/(pr ))n and let S be the trivial brace Z/(pr ).
Let α : (S, ·) −→ Aut(T, +, ·) be the map defined by α(µ) = αµ and

                                         αµ (~x) = f µ (~x),

for all µ ∈ S and ~x ∈ T . It is clear that α is a homomorphism of groups. We
will check that α and −b satisfy condition (1). Since −b is a symmetric bilinear
form, this condition is equivalent to −b(~x, ~y ) = −b(αµ (~x), αµ (~y )), which is true
because f is in the orthogonal group of Q. Let H ′ (pr , n, −b, f ) = T ⋊◦ S be the
asymmetric product of T by S via −b and α.

Proposition 6.1 The map ϕ : H(pr , n, Q, f ) −→ H ′ (pr , n, −b, f ) defined by
ϕ(~x, µ) = (~x, µ − Q(~x)) is an isomorphism of left braces.

Proof. Let ~x, ~y ∈ T and µ, µ′ ∈ S. We have

           ϕ((~x, µ) + (~y , µ′ )) = ϕ(~x + ~y , µ + µ′ )
                                   = (~x + ~y, µ + µ′ − Q(~x + y~))
                                   = (~x + ~y, µ + µ′ − b(~x, ~y ) − Q(~x) − Q(~y ))
                                   = (~x, µ − Q(~x)) + (~y , µ′ − Q(~y))
                                   = ϕ(~x, µ) + ϕ(~y , µ′ )




                                                  25
and
   ϕ((~x, µ) · (~y , µ′ ))
                   = ϕ(~x + f µ−Q(~x) (~y ), µ + µ′ + b(~x, f µ−Q(~x) (~y )))
                   = (~x + f µ−Q(~x) (~y ), µ + µ′ + b(~x, f µ−Q(~x) (~y)) − Q(~x + f µ−Q(~x) (~y )))
                   = (~x + f µ−Q(~x) (~y ), µ + µ′ − Q(~x) − Q(f µ−Q(~x) (~y )))
                   = (~x + f µ−Q(~x) (~y ), µ + µ′ − Q(~x) − Q(~y))
                   = (~x, µ − Q(~x)) · (~y , µ′ − Q(~y))
                   = ϕ(~x, µ) · ϕ(~y , µ′ ).
Thus the result follows.

   Consider now the left brace H1 ⊲⊳ . . . ⊲⊳ Hs described in [6, Theorem 3.6].

    By [6, Theorem 3.6] the left brace H1 ⊲⊳ . . . ⊲⊳ Hs is simple if and only if
ci − id is an automorphism for all 1 ≤ i ≤ s.
    Let T ′ be the trivial brace (Z/(pr11 ))n1 × · · · × (Z/(prss ))ns and let S ′ be the
trivial brace Z/(pr11 ) × · · · × Z/(prss ). Let α′ : (S ′ , ·) −→ Aut(T ′ , +, ·) be the map
defined by α′ (µ1 , . . . , µs ) = α′(µ1 ,...,µs ) and
                                                                              µ

for all (µ1 , . . . , µs ) ∈ S ′ and (~x1 , . . . , ~xs ) ∈ T ′ . Let b′ : T ′ × T ′ −→ S ′ be the
map defined by

               b′ ((~x1 , . . . , ~xs ), (~y1 , . . . , ~ys )) = (−b1 (~x1 , ~y1 ), . . . , −bs (~xs , ~ys )),

for all (~x1 , . . . , ~xs ), (~y1 , . . . , ~ys ) ∈ T ′ . We will check that α′ and b′ satisfy condi-
tion (1). Since b′ is a symmetric bilinear form this is equivalent to

 b′ ((~x1 , . . . , ~xs ), (~y1 , . . . , ~ys )) = b′ (α′(µ1 ,...,µs ) (~x1 , . . . , ~xs ), α′(µ1 ,...,µs ) (~y1 , . . . , ~ys )),

which is true because, for 1 ≤ i < s, ci and fi are in the orthogonal group of
Qi , fs is in the orthogonal group of Qs and

bs (cs (~xs ), cs (~ys )) = Qs (cs (~xs ) + cs (~ys )) − Qs (cs (~xs )) − Qs (cs (~ys ))
                            = Qs (cs (~xs + ~ys )) − Qs (cs (~xs )) − Qs (cs (~ys ))
                            = Qs (~xs + ~ys ) + vs (~xs + y~s )t − Qs (~xs ) − vs ~xts − Qs (~ys ) − vs ~yst
                            = Qs (~xs + ~ys ) − Qs (~xs ) − Qs (~ys )
                            = bs (~xs , ~ys ).

Let B = T ′ ⋊◦ S ′ be the asymmetric product of T ′ by S ′ via b′ and α′ .

Theorem 6.2 The map ϕ′ : H1 ⊲⊳ . . . ⊲⊳ Hs −→ B defined by

           ϕ′ (~x1 , µ1 , . . . , ~xs , µs ) = (~x1 , . . . , ~xs , µ1 − Q1 (~x1 ), . . . , µs − Qs (~xs ))

is an isomorphism of left braces.

Proof. The proof is straightforward using the definitions of the sum and the
multiplication in both left braces and the formula (10).
